label: DGA domains
description: https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1568/002/

label: Domain name compromise
description: The wrongfully taking control of a domain name from the rightful name holder. Compromised domains can be used for different kinds of malicious activity like sending spam or phishing, for distributing malware or as botnet command and control - https://www.icann.org/groups/ssac/documents/sac-007-en.

label: Lame delegations
description: Lame delegations occur as a result of expired nameserver domains allowing attackers to take control of the domain resolution by re-registering this expired nameserver domain - https://blog.apnic.net/2021/03/16/the-prevalence-persistence-perils-of-lame-nameservers/.

label: DNS Cache Poisoning
description: also known as DNS spoofing, is a type of cyber attack in which an attacker corrupts a DNS resolver's cache by injecting false DNS records, causing the resolver to records controlled by the attacker - https://capec.mitre.org/data/definitions/142.html

label: DNS rebinding
description: a type of attack where a malicious website directs a client to a local network address, allowing the attacker to bypass the same-origin policy and gain access to the victim's local resources - https://capec.mitre.org/data/definitions/275.html

label: DNS server compromise
description: DNS server compromise involves unauthorized control over, or access to, a legitimate DNS server, its configuration, or its records. Administrative privileges are not always required. This can enable adversaries to redirect traffic, manipulate queries, force the server to return malicious IP addresses, and launch other cyberattacks. Affected servers can include open recursive DNS servers, authoritative DNS servers, organizational recursive DNS servers, and ISP-operated recursive DNS servers.

label: Stub resolver hijacking
description: The attacker compromises the Operating System of a computer or a phone with malicious code that intercepts and responds to DNS queries with rogue or malicious responses

label: Local recursive resolver hijacking
description: Consumer Premise Equipment (CPE), such as home routers, often provide DNS recursion on the local network. If the CPE device is compromised, the attacker can change the recursive resolver behavior; for example, by changing responses.

label: On-path DNS attack
description: “Attackers intercept communication between a user and a DNS server and provide different destination IP addresses pointing to malicious sites.” (https://www.imperva.com/learn/application-security/dns-hijacking-redirection/)

label: DoS Against the DNS
description: Multiple systems sending malicious traffic to a target at the same time, or attacks against individual targets that prevent DNS service being provided.

label: DNS as a vector for DoS
description: "Adversaries may attempt to cause a denial of service by reflecting a high-volume of network traffic to a target. This type of Network DoS takes advantage of a third-party server intermediary that hosts and will respond to a given spoofed source IP address. This third-party server is commonly termed a reflector. An adversary accomplishes a reflection attack by sending packets to reflectors with the spoofed address of the victim.” “Two prominent protocols that have enabled Reflection Amplification Floods are DNS and NTP though the use of several others in the wild have been documented." These Reflection and Amplification Floods can be directed against components of the DNS, like authoritative nameservers, rendering them unresponsive. (https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1498/002/)

label: Obfuscation via Dynamic DNS
description: Adversaries may dynamically establish connections to command and control infrastructure to evade common detections and remediations. This may be achieved by using malware that shares a common algorithm with the infrastructure the adversary uses to receive the malware's communications. These calculations can be used to dynamically adjust parameters such as the domain name, IP address, or port number the malware uses for command and control. (https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1568/)

label: Fast flux
description: “Adversaries may use Fast Flux DNS to hide a command and control channel behind an array of rapidly changing IP addresses linked to a single domain resolution. This technique uses a fully qualified domain name with multiple IP addresses assigned to it which are swapped with high frequency using a combination of round robin IP addressing and short Time-To-Live (TTL) for a DNS resource record.” (https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1568/001/) "Double fast flux" is where both A/AAAA and NS records are updated to further hide malicious activity.

label: Infiltration and exfiltration via the DNS
description: Exfiltration via the DNS requires a delegated domain or, if the domain does not exist in the public DNS, the operation of a resolver preloaded with that domain's zone file information and configured to receive and respond to the queries sent by the compromised devices.

label: Malicious registration of (effective) second level domains
description: For example, before attacking a victim, adversaries purchase or register domains from an ICANN-accredited registrar that can be used during targeting. See also CAPEC-630.

label: Creation of Malicious Subdomains Under Dynamic DNS Providers
description: Dynamic DNS (DDNS) works by keeping DNS records updated with the correct IP address for a domain. Dynamic DNS providers typically allow users to create subdomains under domains they own. A customer may also use a domain they own with a DDNS provider; however, this technique covers malicious subdomains under provider-owned domains, not customer-owned domains. Before attacking a victim, adversaries create such subdomains through a Dynamic DNS provider, an entity other than a registrar or registry. Providers often offer an API to generate subdomains programmatically, making it easy to create many fully qualified domains for scalable phishing, malware, and other campaigns. These domains can support malicious activity without registering a domain with an entity covered by, for example, the ICANN terms of use. See also https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_DNS.

label: Compromise of a non-DNS server to conduct abuse
description: Internet attack infrastructure is a broad category, and this covers any non-DNS server. Many compromised servers, such as web servers or mail servers, interact with the DNS or may be instrumental in conducting DNS abuse. For example, compromised mail servers are one technique that may be used to send phishing emails.

label: Use of an unregistered domain
description: In a context where a domain name is expected (such as the From header in mail or a URL in a web page or message body), supplying a domain name not controlled by the attacker and that is not controlled by or registered to a legitimate registrant.

label: Spoofing of a registered domain
description: In a context where a domain name is expected (such as the From header in mail or a URL in a web page or message body), supplying a domain name not controlled by the attacker and that is in fact controlled by or registered to a legitimate registrant.

label: DNS tunneling
description: DNS tunneling is the use of DNS network protocols to encapsulate other protocols. The client encodes and sends requests and responses to a server that accepts DNS requests, translates or decodes the DNS traffic, and converts it to the target protocol. DNS tunneling can be used for command and control (C2) communication and as a functional equivalent of a virtual private network. DNS tunneling could also be used for [exfiltration and infiltration](infiltration-and-exfiltration-via-the-dns). Exfiltration and infiltration of information via DNS are addressed separately to account for their different approaches to detection and prevention. DNS traffic may be allowed before network authentication is complete. See also https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071/004/.

label: DNS Beacons - C2 Communication
description: Some kinds of malware send periodic DNS queries to command and control (C2) servers. These periodic communications are known as beacons. DNS beacons can be used to re-establish control over malware, as a form of keepalive for infected hosts, or a low-bandwidth form of C2 communication.
